title: UL for Talking Toys: Behavioral Safety Lab
one_liner: An independent lab that red-teams AI toys and kid-facing companion gadgets with child personas, then sells scorecards and a 'passed' seal to brands and retailers.
customer: AI-toy brands and ODMs launching in the US, licensors of kids' IP, and big-box and online retailers' product-safety and legal teams, plus toy-industry insurers.
problem: Physical toy labs test lead and choking hazards but nobody tests what a toy says across a 200-turn conversation, whether guardrails drift, where audio goes, or whether privacy claims are true. Late-2025 consumer testing reportedly found AI toys giving inappropriate content (not verified in the brief). Retailers carry the liability, and the FTC's 6(b) inquiry, SB 243 and the amended COPPA rule raise the stakes.
solution: A standard suite of about 300 child-persona conversations (ages 4-12, varied accents), child-style jailbreak probing, sensitive-topic sweeps, long-horizon persona drift, network capture of data flows and retention, and verification of COPPA claims. Deliverables are a scorecard, fix list, re-test and a versioned seal retailers can require.
why_now: Holiday 2026 is the first mass AI-toy season (Mattel-OpenAI partnership, from memory; Character.AI's under-18 exit), and retailers' legal teams need evidence by Q4. The buying window is right now.
revenue_model: $12-40k per product per version, annual retainers for brands, and seal licensing fees.
non_obvious_insight: Retailers, not parents, are the choke point, and they buy assurance rather than products. The test is dynamic (behavior over time) rather than static (materials), which makes it a new category of lab created by regulators' fear.
first_30_days: Buy 10 AI toys and gadgets (about $1.5k) and publish a public holiday AI-toy behavior report with methodology. Send private reports to 5 retailer compliance heads and 10 brands. Offer paid re-tests to any brand that fails.

title: Sundowning Night Companion Speaking in Family's Voice
one_liner: A bedside device that detects night waking and reorients a person with dementia in a voice they consented to, escalating to a caregiver or remote night aide.
customer: Family caregivers of people with moderate dementia at home (about 15% provide 60+ hours a week), memory-care communities with thin night ratios, and home-care agencies with overnight cases.
problem: Night waking is a top reason families place a loved one. Overnight aides cost $300-450 a night, and families otherwise absorb 3 am crises. Generic AI companions are seen as deceptive or are not built for dementia.
solution: A bedside speaker or tablet with radar or audio wake detection plays short, clinically scripted reorientation lines in a familiar voice (for example a spouse or child), seeded by a 'voice will' the person records and approves while they still have capacity. It escalates to the caregiver's phone with two-way voice, then to a paid remote night aide, and logs sleep patterns for the neurologist. Guardrails: no impersonation of the deceased, and clinician sign-off.
why_now: Voice cloning from seconds of audio and on-device speech models are cheap in 2026. NY, FL and NJ are giving away ElliQ, showing public payers buy companionship tech, and 23% of 65+ now use ChatGPT, so acceptance is rising.
revenue_model: $199 hardware plus $39-59 a month for families, $30-50 per bed per month for memory care, and remote night-aide add-on fees.
non_obvious_insight: Ethics is the product: an advance 'voice will' turns a controversial deception into a consented comfort, like an advance directive for how you want to be soothed. Night is the least automated and most expensive shift.
first_30_days: Build on a commodity smart speaker with scripted lines, recruit 10 families through Alzheimer's support groups and one neurologist, and measure night-waking events over four weeks. Convene a geriatric psychiatrist and an ethicist as advisors.

title: Technique Capture for Cell Therapy Tech Transfer
one_liner: Instrumented video-and-sensor capture of the 'artisanal' manual steps in cell therapy processes, turned into numeric parameters and training packages for CDMO tech transfer.
customer: Cell and gene therapy developers moving from academic or pilot scale to a CDMO, CDMO MSAT teams, and automation vendors as secondary buyers.
problem: Roughly 10% of a ~5,000-action biomanufacturing workflow is manual and resists automation, for example cell resuspension. The know-how sits in one technician's hands. As cell therapies scale and CDMOs cut staff, process know-how is getting lost in tech transfer. Failed transfers burn months and millions. Cellares' 168 layoffs after BMS ended the partnership show automation capex is fragile.
solution: A 'Technique Package': multi-angle video with hand and pose tracking, Bluetooth pipettes and force or flow sensors, timing, and cell-state images at each critical manual step. Convert it into acceptable ranges, failure signatures, operator training clips and a comparability protocol, delivered before CDMO engineering runs. With customer consent, the data doubles as a physical-AI training set.
why_now: The 5,000-action and 10% artisanal figures come from 2026 GEN reporting. CDMO staff cuts are eroding institutional knowledge. Cheap wearables and egocentric-video models are mature. Transfyr's $25M seed proves investor appetite for the underlying data but targets a different buyer.
revenue_model: $25-120k per transfer package, per-operator training licenses, and data licensing with revenue share.
non_obvious_insight: Sold as tech-transfer insurance (avoid failed engineering runs), not as automation. It needs no robot, no capex and no bet on which automation vendor survives. Buyers pay from the transfer budget, which is already allocated.
first_30_days: Build the kit from off-the-shelf parts. Offer two CGT startups planning CDMO transfers a $20-25k pilot. Capture three high-variance steps and document before-and-after run success.

title: GitHub Outage Hot-Standby Forge
one_liner: A managed Forgejo standby that continuously mirrors repos, PRs, issues and Actions workflows, runs monthly failover drills, and lets a team ship a hotfix in minutes when GitHub is down, so nobody has to migrate off GitHub.
customer: Engineering teams of 5-200 with on-call rotations and release SLAs (B2B SaaS, fintech, agencies), plus EU firms who want a sovereignty story. They pay $8-12 per developer per month, or $99/month flat for teams of 10 or fewer.
problem: Ask HN 'Alternatives to GitHub' hit 649 points and 437 comments on 17 August 2026: 'Github has been down consistently over the last few months'; one team 'had to delay a release due to Github being down'; another said GitHub exceeded in two months a downtime budget its self-hosted GitLab had used only 1.5 days of in six years. The blockers cited for actually leaving are GitHub Actions lock-in, the PR workflow and ecosystem, not git hosting. Teams that do leave need 1-3 people to run a forge.
solution: A GitHub App that syncs code, tags, releases, and (read-write for a defined subset) PRs and issues into a managed per-customer Forgejo instance. A workflow portability linter tells the customer which of their Actions workflows will fail on Forgejo runners and proposes patches. Secrets are synced opt-in and encrypted. A break-glass switch redirects the deploy pipeline to standby runners (Forgejo v15 runs Kubernetes-native ephemeral runners). Monthly automated fire drills execute the customer's real deploy against staging in standby and produce a dated 'last successful failover' badge and status page for customers' security questionnaires.
why_now: GitHub instability through 2026, Forgejo Actions now described by users as 'near 1:1' with GitHub Actions, Forgejo v15's runner improvements (August 2026), and an AI-coding PR and CI volume surge that makes every hour of downtime costlier.
revenue_model: Per-developer subscription ($8-12/dev/month), $99/month flat for small teams, plus runner-minute overage and an enterprise tier with EU-only hosting and SSO.
non_obvious_insight: The 437-comment thread is framed as 'leave GitHub', but the stated blockers mean most teams will not, so the product that gets paid for is insurance rather than migration. Insurance is priced on drill evidence: a dated failover-drill badge is what a CTO can show a customer's procurement team. The open-source workflow linter is the wedge. Evidence: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49331033 (outage complaints, Actions as primary blocker, 'delay a release'); Forgejo Actions compatibility claims and DIY setups costing $60/month for a Kubernetes cluster https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=48473170 and https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49360197.
first_30_days: Release a free open-source CLI that scores a repo's Actions workflows for Forgejo portability and post it in the GitHub-alternatives thread. Stand up a multi-tenant Forgejo with mirror sync in a few weeks using existing Forgejo, its runner and a sync service. Offer a $99/month founding-customer plan to the commenters who delayed releases and to 20 SaaS teams with uptime SLAs. Run the first joint failover drill with each design partner in week 4.

title: Nonrenewal Cure: Rebutting Insurer Cancellations
one_liner: Nonrenewal notices often cite fixable issues like roof condition, tree overhang or debris. Sell homeowners a fast diagnosis, repair and evidence packet to get re-underwritten instead of dumped on a FAIR plan.
customer: Homeowners in CA, FL, TX, CO, UT and NM who have received a nonrenewal notice, plus independent brokers who lose those clients.
problem: Nonrenewals are at records and homeowners have 30-75 days to react. Carriers are structurally conflicted about helping, and the FAIR plan is pricey with thin cover. Homeowners can't decode the reason code, can't tell which items are cheap to fix, and can't produce the evidence a carrier re-inspection accepts.
solution: Upload the notice. The service decodes the stated reason using state disclosure rules, dispatches vetted local contractors for the fix (patch, trim, vent screens), and produces a time-stamped photo and invoice packet. It files for reinspection or appeal, and gives the broker a clean file to re-market the risk. For wildfire-score cases it documents mitigation credits available under state rules.
why_now: Record nonrenewals, California passed three claims and nonrenewal bills on 2026-09-03, and insurance now rivals mortgage payments. Carriers rely more on aerial-imagery flags that homeowners rarely see or contest.
revenue_model: $149 diagnostic, $250-$500 evidence packet, 10-15% contractor referral fee, and broker referral fees on re-placed policies.
non_obvious_insight: Many cancellations are cheap to cure, but the homeowner has no language, time or evidence, and the carrier won't help. A homeowner who has just been rescued becomes a lifetime referral source for brokers.
first_30_days: Post in local nonrenewal threads and neighborhood groups, and partner with three independent brokers. Handle 20 cases by hand, track how many carriers reinstate, and use the win rate to set pricing.

title: Business Identity Watch: LifeLock for LLCs
one_liner: Continuous monitoring of the state filings, liens and listings that define a small business, with a fast response kit when someone hijacks them.
customer: Owners of LLCs and sole proprietorships, reached through community banks, insurance agents, CPAs and registered-agent companies.
problem: Formation is cheap and online, and US domestic companies no longer file beneficial-ownership reports (FinCEN's final rule, August 2026). Census restated its formation series and excluded internet-sales-linked applications from some series, which suggests formation counts are polluted by non-real businesses (inference). Fraudsters can file fake officer or agent changes, register lookalike LLCs and domains, hijack listings and file bogus liens. Owners find out when a collections letter arrives.
solution: Monitor Secretary of State filings across states with open bulk feeds, UCC indexes, lookalike entity names and domains, and Google Business Profile edits. Alert the owner and provide pre-drafted correction filings, fraud affidavits, a registered-agent switch, and a bank notification letter.
why_now: There is no federal ownership registry to lean on, formation is cheap, and AI makes synthetic-identity and lookalike-business fraud cheaper to run.
revenue_model: $9-19 per entity per month, a $299 incident-response fee, and bulk banking deals at about $2 per entity per month.
non_obvious_insight: The state filing is the root of trust for a small business, and nobody watches it. Identity-theft companies watch people, not entities, and a bank that already knows the business is the natural distributor.
first_30_days: Pick five states with open bulk filing data and build change alerts. Pilot with 200 LLCs through one community bank or bookkeeper. Track fraud events detected and time to resolve.

title: Playable-Until Guarantees for Online Games
one_liner: Sell publishers a pre-funded shutdown trust plus an escrowed server kit, so a dated playability guarantee becomes a selling point for $70-80 online games instead of a legal risk.
customer: Indie and mid-size publishers (10-300 staff) of co-op and live-service titles on Steam and console, and premium online games priced at $70-80.
problem: Publishers treat any end-of-life promise as a liability admission, so buyers get none. Anthem shut down on 2026-01-12, and of 738 tracked shutdown games 68% are unplayable or at risk. The EU Commission declined a mandatory rule on 2026-06-16 but wants a voluntary code by end of 2026. UFC-Que Choisir sued Ubisoft over The Crew, and a suit against Sony followed in Aug 2026.
solution: A 'Last Light' package with three parts. (1) Escrow of a server-emulator kit, builds and docs, verified by a clean-room restore drill we run. (2) A small per-title trust funded at launch (1-2% of gross) that pays a hosting partner to keep a minimal community server up for N years. (3) A store-page badge with a date, plus a public verification page. If a sunset trigger fires, the kit is released to the community.
why_now: The EU voluntary code of conduct due by end of 2026 will set a de facto standard that needs an auditor. The Stop Killing Games petition has 1.29M verified signers, a ready-made audience. $70-80 pricing needs a value story, and the Ubisoft and Sony suits show the cost of staying silent.
revenue_model: Certification and restore-drill fee of $8-40k per title, 15-20% admin retention on trust contributions, and $3-5k annual re-certification.
non_obvious_insight: A bounded, dated, funded promise caps liability, while silence leaves it open-ended and now litigated. Most online games reduce to stateless auth and matchmaking, so the guarantee is cheap to keep. Publishers also get a marketing asset that the Stop Killing Games community will actively promote.
first_30_days: Recruit volunteer engineers from the Stop Killing Games community to draft a reference escrow spec. Pitch 30 indie co-op publishers with launches in the next 12 months. Run a free restore drill on one willing title and publish it as a case study. Presell 3 pilots at $5-8k, and get a hosting-partner letter of intent and a lawyer-reviewed template.

title: Delay Insurance for Data Center Energization
one_liner: Parametric insurance and pricing data that pay developers and lenders when the utility misses its committed energization date.
customer: Data center developers, construction lenders and hyperscale tenants with delivery-date penalties. Reinsurers supply the capital.
problem: A delayed 60 MW site costs about $14M a month. Utilities commit to dates that slip, standard delay-in-start-up cover excludes utility delay, and developers cannot hedge the largest schedule risk in the AI buildout.
solution: Build a database of utility energization performance (committed versus actual dates) by utility and substation type. Write parametric cover with the trigger set at the utility's committed date plus N days, under an MGA or coverholder structure with a Lloyd's or reinsurance backer. Also sell a 'time-to-power index' to lenders and developers.
why_now: The hyperscale pipeline is huge, waits reach years, and new large-load tariffs formalize committed dates, so the risk is finally observable in public filings.
revenue_model: Premium of roughly 2-5% of limit a year, with 15-20% MGA commission, plus data subscriptions from lenders and developers.
non_obvious_insight: Delay looks uninsurable only until you notice it is parametric. The trigger is the utility's own date, which the developer cannot move, and it is currently priced by gut.
first_30_days: Compile a dataset from ~200 public PUC and utility large-load filings. Publish a free 'Time-to-Power Index' teaser. Meet three MGAs or coverholders. Pitch 10 lenders. Land one design-partner letter of intent.

title: Aid-in-Dying Program-in-a-Box for Hospices
one_liner: Sell newly-legal states' hospices and health systems the policies, forms, trained consulting-clinician panel and logistics they need to participate in medical aid in dying.
customer: Independent hospices, palliative practices and non-religious health systems in Illinois and New York, then Massachusetts and Pennsylvania if they pass. The buyer is the medical director or administrator.
problem: Legalization creates a right on paper. The bottleneck is willing, trained clinicians (attending plus consulting physician, and mental-health evaluation where required), statutory documentation, waiting periods, pharmacy sourcing and staff opt-out policies. Most providers have no playbook, so patients bounce between systems that opt out. Advocacy groups cover navigation, not staffing.
solution: A turnkey program: policy templates, staff training, state-specific e-documentation workflows, an on-call roster of trained consulting physicians and evaluators (licensed per state, telehealth where allowed), pharmacy coordination, family support, and post-death reporting. The service serves only patient-initiated requests and supports providers that opt in.
why_now: New York's law was signed Feb 6, 2026, and Illinois's law, signed Dec 12, 2025, takes effect this month (Sept 2026). Two large states are opening within months, with 14 jurisdictions now having some form of law and more pending. Scheduled deaths also create planning lead time that sudden deaths never had.
revenue_model: $15-40K program onboarding fee, $500-$1,000 per consult or evaluation, and per-case coordination fees. State grants are possible.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce input is not legal permission but willing clinicians and paperwork bandwidth, so the money is in clinical capacity and compliance, which advocacy nonprofits don't provide.
first_30_days: Sign 2-3 physicians with prior Oregon or Washington experience as advisors. Approach 10 independent Illinois hospices. Sell a $7.5K readiness assessment plus policy pack first. Start recruiting a consulting-physician roster and get counsel to confirm state rules on telehealth and referral fees.

title: Play Yards: Phone-Free Adventure Clubs for Tweens
one_liner: Membership 'junk playground' clubs staffed by trained playworkers for ages 9-14 (tools, timber, fire pits, no phones, no lessons), launched first in four-day-school-week districts where Friday is a childcare hole.
customer: Parents of 9-14-year-olds paying $150-250/month for after-school access or $45-60 per full Friday, plus landlords with vacant retail or barns. Some state child-care subsidies and school-choice funds may help later.
problem: Schools are banning phones and governments are restricting youth social media, but kids have nowhere to go for unstructured, semi-supervised time with peers. Structured enrichment (coding camps, leagues) is oversupplied, while true adventure playgrounds are rare, nonprofit and mostly for younger children.
solution: A leased warehouse, church hall or barn plus a yard, stocked with loose parts, real tools and a fire pit, with a 1:12 playworker-to-child ratio. Ship an insurer-approved risk-benefit policy, playworker training, a phone-locker rule and flexible memberships. Anchor demand with full-day Fridays in four-day-week districts, then add weekday afternoons and holiday camps.
why_now: More than 2,100 public schools in 26 states now run four-day weeks and the number is growing, mostly in rural districts with few child-care options. At the same time school phone bans and the 'anxious generation' movement have made parents ask for offline peer time.
revenue_model: Monthly memberships, per-day Friday fees (about $50 x 35-40 Fridays is roughly $2,000 per child per year), birthday parties, holiday camps, and later franchise or license fees.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce good is not activities, it is unsupervised-feeling time with peers, and what makes it sellable is liability engineering: an insurance-approved risk policy and playwork training that let a for-profit offer what municipalities avoid. Four-day weeks give a ready anchor customer (working parents with an empty Friday) that funds the more interesting weekday model.
first_30_days: Choose a four-day-week district with a supportive superintendent and rent a church hall or barn for about $1k/month. Hire two playworkers, secure a youth-program insurance policy, and pre-sell 25 Friday memberships through school newsletters and Facebook groups. Run four pilot Fridays, gather parent and kid feedback, then add after-school hours.

title: Gig Income Shock Cover From Pooled Data
one_liner: Insure the algorithm: pay drivers when they are deactivated or when regional platform earnings collapse, using pooled earnings data to defeat moral hazard.
customer: Rideshare and delivery drivers through driver co-ops, forums and earnings-tracking apps, and credit unions that finance drivers' cars.
problem: A deactivation or algorithmic pay cut can remove 30-100% of a driver's income overnight with no unemployment insurance, while record auto delinquencies (brief) mean many drivers carry stressed car loans. Individual income insurance has historically failed on moral hazard and adverse selection.
solution: A membership cover paying 2-4 weeks of trailing average earnings on (a) a verified platform deactivation, or (b) a regional earnings-per-hour index falling more than 25% against baseline, computed from pooled, driver-consented earnings data. Structure it through a fronting carrier or discretionary mutual, and offer credit unions a car-payment protection version.
why_now: Record auto delinquencies, growing algorithmic management of pay, driver data cooperatives and earnings-tracking apps that already pool consented data, and instant payout rails.
revenue_model: $10-$20 per month premium, credit-union-paid group premium bundled with car loans, and anonymized index data licensing.
non_obvious_insight: Moral hazard is the classic reason income insurance fails, but a platform-controlled event (deactivation) and a pooled regional index are not something the worker can game. The data cooperatives already exist and are the missing underwriting input.
first_30_days: Partner with one driver co-op or large forum for a 300-member paid pilot with a capped reserve. Collect earnings-data consents, back-test the index triggers on historical data, and have a fronting partner review the structure.

title: Customs-Verified Collateral for Inventory Lenders
one_liner: An API and reporting layer that verifies borrowers' in-transit inventory against ISF, entry, release and liquidation records, so lenders stop financing containers that do not exist.
customer: Inventory-finance and revenue-based lenders for e-commerce brands, factoring companies, ABL desks at small banks, and buyers of tariff-refund receivables. They pay per verification and per monitored loan.
problem: Lenders finance purchase orders and goods on the water. Their collateral evidence is invoices, a bill of lading PDF and the borrower's word. Fraud, double-pledging, inflated quantities and phantom shipments are a chronic loss driver in small-business trade finance. Tariffs made it worse: duties now consume a big share of landed cost, so lenders need to know what was actually declared, at what value, and whether it cleared or is held. The truth exists in CBP data that brokers see within hours. Lenders see it, if at all, weeks late through the borrower.
solution: Connect to the collateral through consent-based data paths: importer-scheduled ACE reports forwarded to a dedicated inbox, and ABI/status feeds from cooperating brokers that get paid for sharing. Reconcile each financed PO against ISF filing, entry summary, release or hold status, declared value and HTS, and (after the IEEPA ruling) refund eligibility. Deliver a loan-level 'entry-verified' status and exception alerts, such as a container that never had an ISF, a value mismatch, or an exam hold that makes collateral illiquid. The same engine verifies IEEPA refund claims for lenders advancing against them.
why_now: Inventory financing and tariff-duty financing for e-commerce brands surged in 2024-26, and lenders are absorbing losses they do not yet understand. Refund-backed lending is new since the Feb 2026 IEEPA ruling and CAPE, and it needs entry-level verification. ACE reports are self-serve, so no permission from CBP is needed. Brokers are looking for revenue beyond thin filing fees.
revenue_model: $15-40 per shipment verification, or a monitoring SaaS fee of about 5-15 basis points on funded volume, with platform minimums of $2-5k a month. Brokers get a revenue share on data feeds. Add-on: refund-claim diligence packages.
non_obvious_insight: A PO and a bill of lading are easy to forge. An ISF filed before vessel loading, tied to a bond, followed by a release message from CBP, is not. It is the closest thing to a government-attested proof that goods exist and are moving. Because the importer owns the ACE data, no data-broker licensing fight is needed. Trade-finance software vendors model documents. Nobody models the entry record.
first_30_days: Approach five small inventory lenders, factors and refund-claim buyers with a manual pilot: they send 10 borrowers' entry data, and you return verified and unverified lists within 48 hours. Recruit two friendly customs brokers for feed access on consenting clients. Build the reconciliation on spreadsheets and scripts first, and charge $500-$1,500 per pilot batch. The first paid lender contract is usually a covenant addition: 'borrower must forward ACE reports monthly'.

title: Off-the-Record Governance for AI Meeting Transcripts
one_liner: A policy layer over Zoom, Teams and Meet notetakers that decides what becomes 'the record'. It auto-pauses for privileged talk, purges verbatim transcripts once counsel-approved minutes are certified, and blocks unauthorized bots.
customer: General counsel and compliance leads at regulated mid-market companies with 200-5,000 employees, such as healthcare systems, fintechs, biotechs and defense contractors. Also law firms and corporate secretaries who run board minutes.
problem: AI notetakers made every meeting a verbatim, discoverable and error-prone transcript by default. A wrong attribution, such as 'we knew' instead of 'we know,' can become an exhibit. Third-party bots joining privileged calls raise waiver risk. Recording-consent class actions against AI notetaker vendors are rising, especially in all-party-consent states. General counsel have no control primitive between 'record everything' and 'ban notetakers.'
solution: A meeting-level record mode with three states: on the record, off the record and privileged. It is enforced through calendar tags, participant signals (a lawyer joins, so transcript is suppressed) and admin APIs for Microsoft 365 and Google Workspace. Verbatim transcripts carry retention timers (7-30 days, unless a legal hold applies). A named human designee approves a summary, which becomes the sole record with an attestation stamp modeled on a reporter's certificate. Add an audit log and a bot allow-list. It sits on top of the notetakers the company already uses.
why_now: Enterprises spent 2025-26 rolling out Copilot, Gemini and Zoom AI notes company-wide. Lawsuits over AI notetaker recording consent were filed in 2025. Regulators have punished off-channel record-keeping failures, so record governance is now a board-level topic. Legal teams are asking for controls now.
revenue_model: $6-$12 per user per month with a $25,000 annual minimum. An entry 'Record Risk Audit' as a fixed $5,000-$10,000 project that converts to the platform. A channel through employment and litigation law firms that advise clients on AI policy.
non_obvious_insight: Reporters live by one ritual, 'off the record,' a physical control (they stop writing) that AI notetakers lack. They also know that outside a proceeding a verbatim transcript is a liability, not an asset. Most companies are only now realizing they built a huge discoverable archive of casual speech.
first_30_days: Sell the $5,000 audit to 10 general counsel through ACC chapters and LinkedIn. Inventory each company's bot footprint from admin logs and deliver a policy template. Build a thin MVP using Microsoft Graph and Google admin APIs that flips transcription per meeting from calendar tags. Convert 3 audits into paid pilots.

title: Rent Ledger for Adult Kids Living at Home
one_liner: A simple lease, payment and credit-reporting layer that lets parents charge their adult children rent, build the kids' credit history, and quietly bank the money as a down-payment fund.
customer: Parents (Gen X and Boomers) with adult children aged 22-30 living at home, paying $12/month per household. Secondary revenue from mortgage lenders and first-time-buyer programs.
problem: Nearly half (49%) of US adults under 30 lived with parents in 2025, up 12 percentage points from 2019 (Federal Reserve SHED). Only 63% of adults could cover a $400 emergency with cash or a paid-off card, and the Fed reports 16% of adults use buy-now-pay-later, with 11% of users hit by overdraft fees from missed payments. Lender-side data shows BNPL is spreading into groceries (a LendingTree survey reported nearly a quarter of BNPL users financed groceries, up from 14%; 41% reported a late payment). These young adults are paying for hobbies, subscriptions and installment plans while accruing no rent history at all, since informal family housing builds no credit and no savings discipline.
solution: An app that produces a simple parent-child lease, collects a modest monthly 'rent' by ACH, reports on-time payments to the credit bureaus through an established rent-reporting partner (do not become a furnisher), and lets the parent choose to escrow the money in a labeled account toward a future down payment or move-out fund. It gives the kid a monthly statement and a BNPL and subscription view so obligations don't collide with rent day. It includes parent-side documentation of the rent for tax purposes (tax treatment is a gray area, so it needs CPA-reviewed templates).
why_now: The 12-point jump in under-30s living at home is now structural, not a pandemic blip. Rent reporting has been mainstreamed by consumer fintechs and by underwriting systems that count rental payment history, and BNPL late payments are rising, which raises the value of a credibility-building habit. Housing costs make first-time down payments the main goal for these households.
revenue_model: $12/month per household (parent pays), $5/month optional kid add-on for credit-builder features. Referral fees from mortgage lenders and down-payment-assistance programs when the kid buys. Later: employer benefit channel for parents.
non_obvious_insight: Parents are the largest unpriced landlord class in the US, and they already hold the leverage the market lacks: the kid will pay them and will not skip. The product isn't a rent app, it is a behavioral bridge that converts a free-rent arrangement into credit history plus parent-held savings. Evidence: Federal Reserve SHED 2025 https://www.federalreserve.gov/publications/2026-economic-well-being-of-us-households-in-2025-executive-summary.htm (49% of under-30s living with parents, +12 points since 2019; 63% cover $400; 16% BNPL, 11% overdraft fees) and BNPL grocery and late-payment figures via https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buy_now,_pay_later (summarizing LendingTree). Assumptions to validate first: that bureaus and lenders will accept rent reported for a parent-landlord and how underwriting treats it, and that parents want to charge rent and save it. I found no survey on either.
first_30_days: Interview 20 parents in local parenting and finance Facebook groups. Test a landing page and a $12/month waitlist. Run a concierge pilot with 10 families: a lease template, ACH collection, an existing rent-reporting partner and a shared spreadsheet. Confirm with a mortgage broker whether reported parent-landlord rent helps underwriting. Target 15 paying families and one lender-partner conversation.

title: Timed Slots for Viral Fields and Harvest Rescue
one_liner: Ticketing built around bloom and ripeness windows that turns crop-trampling influencers and crew-short fields into capped, paid visitor days.
customer: Specialty and mid-size growers with photogenic or U-pick crops near metros (tulips, lavender, sunflowers, blueberries, peaches, apples, pumpkins), especially those with unharvested acres from crew shortages. Rural tourism boards are a second payer.
problem: Viral fields get trampled while farmers earn nothing, and destinations lack allocation tools (Fuji's hard cap is the model). Meanwhile fruit rotted in fields in 2025 for lack of pickers and late or absent H-2A crews mean lost revenue. Farms squeezed by diesel up 80% and a fourth loss-making row-crop year need any extra income.
solution: Bloom and ripeness forecasts from degree-day models and owner photos drive timed-entry capacity by field zone, waivers, weigh-station POS for pay-per-pound U-pick, and parking and shuttle management. A 'harvest rescue weekend' feature lets a farm that is short of pickers list a paid visitor-harvest event 5-10 days out, with dynamic pricing by forecast and weather. Dispersal nudges route overflow to lesser-known partner farms, and nearby motel beds can be bundled.
why_now: Crew shortages, high input costs and social-media virality are all at peak in 2026, and destinations from Barcelona to Glasgow are moving from fees to allocation. Agritourism liability laws are widespread. Lead times are shortening to about 33 days, so last-minute local trips are growing.
revenue_model: 8-12% of ticket value plus $1.50-$2.50 per ticket in payments. $199/season SaaS for farms. Sponsored dispersal campaigns from tourism boards.
non_obvious_insight: A crop calendar is a supply curve with a 7-14 day peak, so the same forecast tells a farmer when to harvest and a tourist when to come. One dataset prices both the labour gap and the crowd, and U-pick as an emergency labour substitute is a hedge farms already improvise but nobody productises.
first_30_days: Sign 5 orchards and pumpkin farms for immediate October weekend slots to test capacity caps and pricing this month. Then sign 10 farms for spring 2027 tulips and strawberries starting in January, using white-label Stripe ticket pages before building custom software.

title: Philanthropic First-Loss Pool for Vet Care Loans
one_liner: Use foundation money as a loan guarantee instead of a grant, so each philanthropic dollar backs many dollars of low-APR vet credit that recycles as owners repay.
customer: Credit unions and CDFIs (lenders), private foundations (guarantee capital via program-related investments), and clinics (merchant side). End borrowers are middle-income owners who decline care.
problem: The briefing says 13% of euthanasias are attributed to inability to pay, and half of owners would be stressed by a bill of $1,000 or less. Options today are deferred-interest cards with 30%-plus APRs after the promo period, or subprime fintech loans. New philanthropy (Duffield $250M over 5 years; first grants are 250 x $10K) can't fund per-case care one grant at a time.
solution: A 'Care Guarantee Pool': a foundation funds a first-loss reserve (say 10-15% of a loan portfolio). A partner credit union or CDFI originates fixed-rate installment loans of $500-$5,000 at the clinic front desk, and the clinic is paid in about 48 hours. The vet's treatment plan is attached as collateral evidence to limit fraud, with an option to assign insurance proceeds. We run the program: clinic onboarding, application flow, servicing data and outcome reporting ('pets treated instead of euthanized').
why_now: The Duffield Foundation committed $250M on 2026-09-17, on top of PetSmart Charities' $100M pledge. Funders are looking for leverage and measurable outcomes. Embedded-lending rails (bank-as-a-service, instant payouts) make a lender-agnostic origination flow cheap to build.
revenue_model: 1-2% annual program-management fee on guaranteed balances (paid by the foundation), 2-3% origination fee from clinics, and a servicing share from the lender. Later, licensing of performance data.
non_obvious_insight: Philanthropy frames access as a subsidy problem. For the many owners who would repay an $1,800 bill over 12 months at 8% but face 30% APR or a deferred-interest trap, it is a cost-of-capital problem. A guarantee makes a one-shot grant a revolving fund, and it gives funders the proof they crave.
first_30_days: Get an LOI from one credit union or CDFI. Recruit 3 affordable-care clinics in one metro. Pitch a local community foundation and PetSmart Charities for a $250K pilot reserve (roughly $2M of loans). Use the lender's existing loan-origination software plus a simple clinic link. Model expected loss from 12-month payment-plan data at the clinics.

title: Cell-Type-Restricted Promoters for Safer AAV
one_liner: AI-designed, primary-cell-validated regulatory sequences that switch AAV or LNP transgenes on only in target tissues and off in the liver.
customer: Gene therapy developers in muscle, heart and CNS (DMD, LGMD, cardiomyopathies) and capsid or CDMO companies wanting a detargeting cassette.
problem: High-dose systemic AAV caused acute liver failure deaths in 2025: three Sarepta patients, followed by a boxed warning and removal of non-ambulatory eligibility by Nov 14, 2025. Capsid engineering gets the attention, but the expression cassette is a second lever. Common promoters (CMV, CAG) are strong but non-specific, and miR-122 target sites only partly suppress liver expression.
solution: Generative design plus MPRA in iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and skeletal muscle cells and in primary human hepatocytes, ranking 10^4-10^5 sequences for high target and low liver expression. Deliver compact promoter-enhancer sets (under ~500 bp) with an optional miR-detargeting cassette, validated in vitro and in one partner rodent or NHP pilot.
why_now: The 2025 safety crisis is pushing dose reduction and liver detargeting. MPRA and generative sequence models are mature, DNA is cheap, and FDA's move toward human-relevant methods favors human primary-cell data.
revenue_model: $150-300k design-and-validation project plus a $50-200k license, with milestones or light royalties.
non_obvious_insight: The industry over-indexes on capsids, yet toxicity tracks where the transgene is expressed at dose. Compact regulatory parts are modular IP that stacks with any capsid, so one library serves many developers.
first_30_days: Run an MPRA on about 20k designed sequences in iPSC cardiomyocytes versus hepatocytes ($40-60k in reagents and sequencing). Publish a preprint and pitch 15 DMD, LGMD and cardiac programs on $50k pilots.

title: Verification Service for Satellite Imagery Authenticity
one_liner: Check whether a satellite image is real, and issue a chain-of-custody certificate for images used as evidence.
customer: Trade-finance banks and collateral managers, property and cargo insurers, sanctions and compliance teams, and newsroom verification desks.
problem: Generative AI can now fake satellite images, and fakes circulated during conflicts in 2025 (prior knowledge). Imagery is increasingly used as evidence for loans against stockpiles, insurance claims, sanctions cases and environmental claims. Fraud incentives rise with that value, and nobody certifies pixels.
solution: A verification API that checks a submitted image against multi-provider archives (free Sentinel and Landsat plus commercial partners) and physical consistency (sun angle, shadows, sensor geometry). Partners can sign images at ingestion with a provenance manifest. Deliver certified 'as-of' extracts for legal use.
why_now: Generative image quality crossed the threshold in 2025-26. Imagery archives are large and multi-source, and providers are looking for premium 'verified' tiers. The briefing notes decision products for regulated buyers remain open.
revenue_model: $20-200 per verification. Enterprise subscriptions of $30-150k per year. Revenue share with imagery providers on verified tiers.
non_obvious_insight: Detection models age quickly, but archive access does not. The moat is a cross-provider archive and provenance partnerships, not a classifier.
first_30_days: Assemble a test set of real and synthetic images. Build a reverse-lookup against Sentinel-2 and Landsat. Run free verifications for two commodity-finance firms and one newsroom, then convert one to a paid annual license.

title: Disposable Ocean Drifters Reporting Through Orbit
one_liner: $10-30 drifting sensors dropped from passing ships that report through Bluetooth-to-satellite links, building a dense ocean nowcast.
customer: Weather-routing companies, offshore wind and energy operators, hurricane-season shipping and fishing fleets, insurers and coast guards.
problem: Ocean observation is sparse and expensive, because standard buoys cost thousands of dollars each, and some public observing networks have reportedly lost capacity. Routing and offshore-operations customers pay for better current, wave and sea-surface data.
solution: A disposable floating sensor (GPS, temperature, basic wave motion) that uses a standard Bluetooth chip and a Bluetooth-to-satellite network for uplink. Recruit ships of opportunity (research vessels, yacht races, cargo lines) to deploy hundreds. Sell a nowcast layer and event-specific coverage such as hurricane drifts.
why_now: Hubble Network (6 satellites, $200M Series C) shows ordinary Bluetooth chips can reach orbit, and its next generation improves link margins. Sensors and uplink are now cheap enough for disposable use.
revenue_model: Data subscriptions $20-100k per year per routing or offshore customer. Event campaigns of $50-200k. Sensor kits sold at cost to research and racing fleets.
non_obvious_insight: Cheap satellite uplink flips ocean sensing from a few expensive fixed buoys to millions of throwaway ones, and ships already crossing the ocean provide free deployment.
first_30_days: Build 50 prototype drifters and test the link at sea on a partner yacht or research cruise. Sign two weather-routing or offshore wind customers for paid pilots before the next hurricane season.

title: Workup Cover: Insurance for Scan Findings
one_liner: A prepaid guarantee sold at checkout for $800-$1,000 whole-body MRIs and $949 cancer blood tests that covers the second read, the guideline triage and pre-priced follow-up when a scan finds something.
customer: Cash-pay screening buyers 45-70 (whole-body MRI, multi-cancer blood tests, coronary calcium, low-dose CT). First, people who already hold a frightening PDF; second, imaging centers and screening brands that want higher conversion and fewer angry customers; third, concierge doctors and employers.
problem: Screening has gotten cheap enough for the middle class (Function Health's Ezra scan lists at $999 or $799 for members, SimonMed at $899 promotional). The FDA advisory panel voted on September 23, 2026 to back Grail's Galleri blood test, and a new law lets Medicare cover such tests starting in 2028. But the tail is unpriced and unmanaged: in one large study about one in three whole-body MRI participants had an incidental finding and 62% of those biopsied had no malignancy, and the American College of Radiology does not recommend total-body MRI for average-risk adults. The follow-up (specialist visits, repeat imaging, biopsy) is stressful, uncoordinated and can run into the thousands.
solution: An add-on with three layers. (1) A subspecialty radiologist second read within 48 hours. (2) Guideline-based triage (Bosniak, TI-RADS, Fleischner, LI-RADS) that turns the majority of low-risk findings into 'do nothing or repeat in 12 months' with a written explanation. (3) A nurse navigator who books any needed follow-up at pre-negotiated cash prices and, once loss data exist, a financial cap on follow-up costs underwritten with a reinsurer or managing general agent. Phase 1 has no underwriting: sell 'Second Read and Triage' for $149 standalone; Phase 2 adds the guarantee.
why_now: Three things converged in 2025-26: scan prices fell below $1,000 through Function Health and others, the first FDA advisory-panel endorsement of a multi-cancer blood test arrived, and Medicare coverage is scheduled for 2028. Volume of consumer screening is climbing while incidental-finding anxiety is a top complaint in patient communities.
revenue_model: $149-249 attach fee at time of scan purchase (screening seller keeps 20-30% revenue share), $199 standalone second reads, and reinsured guarantee margin: most findings resolve with a read, so expected follow-up payout per member is a small fraction of the fee. Later: protocol licensing to health systems and imaging chains.
non_obvious_insight: The bottleneck to mass preventive screening is not the price of the test but the unpriced tail. Pricing the tail like an extended warranty turns screening's biggest ethical objection (cascades of follow-up) into a product feature, and it lets cheap scans sell without the seller being blamed for the aftermath. A radiology-native underwriter also prices this risk better than a generic insurer.
first_30_days: Recruit three moonlighting subspecialty teleradiologists licensed in target states and one RN navigator. Set up secure image upload with an off-the-shelf DICOM-sharing platform. Launch a $149 'Scary PDF Second Read' in the patient communities around Prenuvo and Function, and sign referral agreements with two independent imaging centers selling $899 MRIs. Log every finding and outcome to price the guarantee. Target 100 second reads in 60 days.

title: Retrain Displaced Managers for Data-Center Builds
one_liner: A 10-week bridge program that turns laid-off program managers, analysts and ops leads into project-controls, cost-estimating, commissioning-paperwork and permitting roles at data-center and grid builders.
customer: General contractors, EPC firms, data-center developers and utility contractors pay a $12-25k placement fee or staff-augmentation margin. Learners pay little, or the cost is covered by workforce-board funds.
problem: Everyone tells displaced office workers to 'learn AI', the most crowded direction. Meanwhile AI's own physical build-out has a shortage of schedulers (P6), cost engineers, document controllers, commissioning coordinators and interconnection or permit analysts. Contractors can't hire them, and mid-career office workers face 6-13 month searches.
solution: Cohort training on scheduling, cost control, contracts, commissioning documentation and site-safety basics, taught by retired project-controls leads. It includes a paid 4-week job-shadow on live projects, certification prep (OSHA 30, PMI-SP, AACE) and guaranteed interviews with partner contractors.
why_now: Hyperscaler capex on data centers and grid work is at record levels and contractors openly cite labor shortages. Big-company cuts of managers ('anti-bureaucracy' layoffs like Amazon's ~16,000) are pushing experienced coordinators onto the market. Stanford data shows the pain concentrated in AI-exposed office roles.
revenue_model: Placement fee of 10-15% of first-year salary (about $12-18k) from contractors, plus paid corporate cohorts and optional deferred tuition.
non_obvious_insight: The AI boom creates a shortage of non-technical, non-AI office roles in the physical world. The displaced manager's scarce skill (vendor wrangling, org navigation, documentation discipline) is exactly what construction lacks, and nobody is training for it.
first_30_days: Call 20 mid-size mechanical and electrical contractors in hot markets (Texas, Virginia, Ohio, Arizona) and get their unfilled-role lists. Sign 3 pay-per-hire LOIs. Recruit 15 laid-off PMs from layoff communities. Run a 4-week evening pilot with a retired scheduler and place the first 5.

title: Unlisted: The Agent-Proof Offline Guide
one_liner: A numbered, mailed-only paper guide plus a human phone line for restaurants, bars, and shops that deliberately cannot be found or booked by AI agents.
customer: Affluent urbanites (30-60) paying $250-400/year, capped at about 2,000 members per city. Corporate concierge and client-gifting accounts pay $5-20k/year. Venues pay nothing, which keeps the guide's independence.
problem: ChatGPT began booking tables through OpenTable, Resy, and Yelp on 10 August 2026, and Gemini, Alexa+, and Perplexity have similar integrations. Everyone's agent now picks the same top-ranked places, bots snipe scarce tables, and Resy prohibits unsanctioned agents. 'I found this place' no longer signals taste, and small venues that want regulars rather than scale have no way to opt out of the flood.
solution: A quarterly printed booklet of 40-60 venues per city, compiled by scouts who visit anonymously. It is posted to members and never published as a PDF. Each entry has a phone number for the Unlisted line, a human-staffed concierge that books by voice, or a door code word, and never an online booking link. Fictional 'canary' details in entries let the guide trace leaks. Members agree to a no-posting norm and are expelled for breaking it. Venues get vetted, lower-no-show clientele.
why_now: Agentic booking went mainstream in August 2026 and venues are reacting with bot bans. Platform algorithms now homogenize discovery. Freelance food and travel writers are being laid off, so scout supply is cheap and high quality.
revenue_model: $250-400/year membership. Corporate concierge accounts. Paid members-only events in venues (ticketed, with the venue's cut waived). Possible city-by-city licensing to local scouts later.
non_obvious_insight: When discovery is automated, unindexability becomes the scarce good. The guide earns trust by refusing to be online, and its scarcity is enforced by physical media and an honor code. Its value is negative space that AI agents structurally cannot see.
first_30_days: Pick one city and hire 3-4 laid-off food writers as scouts. Post a teaser page with no venue names and pre-sell 300 founding memberships at $200. Print 500 numbered copies. Run the phone line on a shared business number with two part-timers. Test the model by having a scout call in a booking.

title: RoboManual: Appliance Manuals Written for Humanoids
one_liner: A licensed library of articulated digital twins and operating procedures (where to press, how the latch moves, how much force) for the 500 most common home appliances, sold to home-robot makers and to appliance brands that want their products to be robot-ready.
customer: Home and general-purpose robot companies and robot foundation-model labs (1X, Figure, Sunday-type startups, Tesla-adjacent teams, lab groups training manipulation policies). Later, appliance OEMs (dishwashers, washers, ovens, fridges) and retailers.
problem: Home humanoids ship into thousands of models of dishwashers, washers, ovens and jars. 1X's Neo, the first humanoid actually delivered to consumers, leans on remote human operators for tasks like laundry and dishes because robots do not know how to operate your specific machine. Appliance makers wrote manuals for humans; nobody owns the equivalent for machines: hinge axes, latch travel, button actuation force, timing and failure modes.
solution: A physical-measurement studio that scans and instruments appliances. It produces articulated 3D assets (URDF/USD) with annotated affordances (press points, required force, latch and door kinematics, common jams) plus step-by-step procedure graphs and video of human demonstrations. Delivered as a dataset license and a lookup API keyed by model number, so a robot can scan a label and retrieve its operating plan. Every deployed robot's failures feed back to update the manual. Appliance OEMs pay for inclusion and a 'robot-graspable' certification.
why_now: Consumer humanoids started shipping in 2026 (1X Neo, $20k or $499/month) and are teleop-assisted, so every learned procedure has a direct dollar value in removed operator hours. Sim-based training pipelines are hungry for articulated real-world assets. Industrial pilots by Figure, Agility and Apptronik make robot makers seek reusable object knowledge.
revenue_model: Dataset licenses of $25-100k per year per lab or robot maker, per-lookup API fees at scale, OEM inclusion and certification fees ($20-50k per product line), and custom scan projects.
non_obvious_insight: Robots do not lack general knowledge about 'a dishwasher'. They lack knowledge about this latch and this button lag. The moat is physical measurement labor plus fleet feedback, not AI, so big labs will not bother to build it early. It is the 'second manual' of the appliance industry.
first_30_days: Partner with a scratch-and-dent appliance outlet and a repair shop for scan access. Capture 50-100 top-selling dishwashers, washers, dryers, microwaves and ovens with photogrammetry, a force gauge and video of human operation. Produce cleaned articulated assets with affordance labels and sell a pilot pack to 2-3 home-robot startups at $25-50k.

title: Weather Forecasts for GPS Jamming
one_liner: A crowd-sensed, forecastable map of GNSS jamming and spoofing for the civil operators nobody warns: survey and RTK fleets, drone operators and marine underwriters.
customer: First: commercial drone operators, RTK survey and construction machine-control fleets, and precision-ag contractors in the Baltics, Poland, Finland, Turkey and the Gulf, at $99 to $499 a month. Second: marine war-risk MGAs, P&I clubs and route planners, at $50k to $250k a year.
problem: Jamming and spoofing have surged (EASA revised its GNSS-interference bulletin again in July 2026; Hormuz and Bab el-Mandeb dominate ship incidents; insurers are bracing for mega-claims). Operators learn about it when a drone flies away or autosteer fails. Public maps such as GPSJam are daily averages built from ADS-B, too coarse for a specific field or route hour.
solution: A sensor network of cheap multi-band GNSS receivers and opted-in Android raw-GNSS phones (hosts are farmers, truckers and drone pilots, paid in free forecasts). It detects carrier-to-noise collapse and spoofing signatures at about 1 km resolution in near real time. On top of that sits a forecast (jammers repeat by hour and geometry) and an API/SMS alert such as 'L1 degraded within 20 km of your flight plan 14:00-16:00'. A signed position-integrity report is offered to insurers.
why_now: Dual-frequency GNSS chips cost about $10 and expose raw measurements. Android exposes raw GNSS data. Jamming intensity rose sharply through 2025-26, and insurers and P&I clubs have started buying authentication tech, so the demand signal is visible in the market.
revenue_model: SaaS of $99 to $999 a month for fleets. Annual data licences of $50k to $250k to insurers and MGAs. Per-report fee for integrity certificates. Optional hardware host kit sold at cost.
non_obvious_insight: Jamming is spatially and temporally patterned like weather, so it can be forecast, not just mapped afterward. The paying buyers are not militaries but civil operators whose exposure nobody prices. The sensor network gets built for free if you pay hosts in forecasts.
first_30_days: Deploy 30 receivers with three agri-drone and survey firms in Poland and the Baltics. Email a weekly jamming map overlaid on their own flight logs. Sign 10 paying users at 99 EUR a month. Send a route-level sample dataset to two marine war-risk underwriters.

title: Notary for AI Agents' Authority to Sign
one_liner: A registry of signed, scoped, revocable 'mandates' that let a company's AI agents prove to counterparties what they may commit to, with a legal opinion and an insurer behind each.
customer: SMBs and mid-market firms deploying purchasing, AR/AP, sales-ops and scheduling agents (finance and ops leads), the fintech and AP-automation platforms embedding those agents, and the vendors on the receiving end.
problem: Agents now email vendors, accept quotes, change orders and click 'I agree'. Counterparties cannot tell whether an agent had authority, whose it is, or its spend limit, and companies cannot prove afterward what they authorized. Contract-formation doctrine (electronic-agent provisions, apparent authority) predates this. Payment protocols carry payment mandates, not authority to bind.
solution: Phase one: a legal template and JSON mandate schema (principal, agent identity, scope by category and counterparty, dollar cap, expiry, escalation), signed as verifiable credentials, with a public verify API and a revocation registry, an audit log, and a law-firm opinion letter on enforceability for the first US states. Any counterparty agent can call a check_mandate MCP tool. Phase two: an MGA-backed insurance product for agent commitments up to the mandate cap.
why_now: MCP and agent-payment protocols emerged in 2025 and small-firm agent adoption is visible now (60+ firms on MyCase's connector in one month), yet the contract-authority layer between payments and law has no owner (background, verify).
revenue_model: $50-500/month per business, per-verification fees for high-volume counterparties, an insurance premium share, and $10-25k enterprise opinion-letter packages.
non_obvious_insight: Payment rails answer 'can this agent pay?' while the law asks 'was it authorized to bind?', and that depends on documented delegation, the same problem powers of attorney and corporate resolutions solved for humans. Whoever sets the schema counterparties check becomes the standard.
first_30_days: Draft the mandate schema and template with a partner law firm and publish an open spec. Pilot with five procurement or AP-agent startups, ship the verify API, get three design partners to put an authority header in agent emails, and open talks with two MGAs.
